source_text:
ART. VI.
An precedens doctrina tollat peccati originalis propagationem.

1. Qui putant humanam animam a DEO immediate non creari, sed ex potentia seminis educi, objicere solent, nostram sententiam plane tollere peccati originalis propagationem, & nullum modum relinquere quo explicari possit istius peccati derivatio a parentibus ad liberos: ut igitur hoc cavillum ipso facto diluam, partes quasi integrantes illius peccati enumerabo, & quomodo singulae propagentur docebo.

2. Partes peccati originalis sunt tres: Primo, participatio peccati primorum parentum; illud enim fuit commune peccatum totius generis humani. Secundo, carentia originalis justitiae, id est, defectus donorum, tum intellectus tum voluntatis, quibus Adamus & Eva ante lapsum ornati sunt. Tertio, propensio vel inclinatio ad malum; non enim solum caremus originali justitia, quae nos ad bonum propensos faciebat, sed etiam a sublata successit contraria qualitas legi adversa, quae nos ad omnem turpitudinem pronos reddit.

3. Prima pars peccati originalis eodem modo propagatur a parentibus ad liberos, quo coloris vel generis splendor, item jus haereditarium: nimirum neque per animam, neque per corpus, sed per naturalem generationem. Sicut enim Carolus, v.g., ideo haeres regni est, quia Regis filius est, & ideo filius Regis, quia a Rege genitus est; sicut etiam Carolus ideo nobilis est, quia nobilium parentum proles est, & ideo proles, quia a nobilibus parentibus per naturalem generationem descendit: ita etiam Adae peccatum ideo est nostrum, quia nos ejus filii & haeredes sumus; i.e. quia per naturalem generationem descendimus ab Adamo. Haec sententia de propagatione primae hujus partis peccati originalis coincidit cum eorum sententia, qui dicunt animam a DEO creatam evadere corruptam & ream per hypostaticam suam unionem cum corpore, quia ex illa unione animae & corporis resultat totus homo, qui est successor Adami, atque adeo reus inobedientiae Adami.

4. Hic tria diligenter notanda sunt: Primo, ea quae jam dicta sunt non esse de quolibet successore Adami, sed de successore per naturalem generationem genito, i.e. de eo, qui per ordinarium modum generandi, videlicet per concursum maris & feminae, ab Adamo descendit; alioqui enim sequeretur Dominum nostrum IESUM CHRISTUM esse reum peccati Adami, quod absurdum & impium dictu est. Secundo notetur, beatam Virginem necessario esse ream peccati Adami; si enim illud ipsum propter quod nos rei sumus peccati Adami, inveniatur in beata Virgine, ipsa non minus est rea quam nos: at verum est prius; illa enim eodem modo descendit ab Adamo quo nos: Ergo etiam verum est posterius.

5. Tertio notetur, solius primi hominis, non vero posteriorum parentum peccata transire in eorum filios: cujus rei ratio praecipue est haec: primus homo justitiam accepit non sibi tantum, sed toti etiam ejus posteritati; ut si permaneret in justitia, eam simul cum natura in posteros transmitteret; sin eam peccando desereret, cum eadem natura labem quoque in omnem posteritatem transfunderet. Cum igitur nemo posteriorum parentum simili lege sit institutus, patet istorum peccata non magis quam justitiam propagari in posteros, sed singularia & (ut loquuntur) personalia tantum esse.

6. Secundam partem peccati originalis, viz. carentiam originalis justitiae, parentes in posteros transmittunt eo modo quo parentes egeni, inglorii, & ignobiles suam egestatem & generis obscuritatem in liberos transfundunt, viz. modo aliquo negativo, non positivo: sicut enim ignobilium & pauperum filii ideo ignobiles sunt & pauperes, quia eorum parentes istis bonis carent, & proinde ea liberis suis conferre nequeunt: ita etiam infans recens natus originali justitia caret, quia parentes ipsius justitia destituti sunt, & proinde eam proli suae communicare nequeunt. Dicet aliquis: parentes fideles, per gratiam restitutionis aliquatenus sibi restituta, cur non ergo ea dona in posteros transfundunt? Resp. quia nulli proximorum parentum, imo ne ipsi Adae, postquam semel peccavit, concessum est ut donum hoc in posteros transmittat; hoc enim concessum est solis primis parentibus ante eorum lapsum.

7. Quod ad tertiam partem peccati originalis attinet, communis sententia est, eam eodem modo propagari & transmitti in liberos, quo lepra transmittitur a parentibus leprosis in eorum liberos, mediante semine ab eis emisso: hoc autem sic declaratur; infectio, quae est in semine leprosi, non est lepra vel esse formaliter & actu, sed solum virtualiter; nam est occulta quaedam dispositio ad lepram: ita etiam infectio spiritualis, quae est in semine, non est peccatum actu & formaliter, sed occulta quaedam dispositio ad peccatum; ex quo fit ut anima in corpore a DEO creata, veluti in loco faedo, a prima sua origine ex corpore vitium contrahat. Hujus rei solidissimum fundamentum est, mutua eaque naturalis sympathia, i.e. passionum & affectionum communicatio, inter corpus & animam, tanquam inter duas partes substantiales idem compositum naturale constituentes. Unde fieri videmus, ut corpore male affecto anima male afficiatur.
english: Article VI. Whether the preceding doctrine abolishes the propagation of original sin.

1. Those who deny that God immediately creates the human soul and hold instead that it is educed from the seed's potency commonly object that our doctrine abolishes original sin's propagation and leaves no way to explain how that sin passes from parents to children. To dissolve the cavil by the fact itself, I will name the quasi-integral parts of that sin and show how each is propagated.

2. Original sin has three parts. First: participation in the first parents' sin — the common sin of the whole human race. Second: lack of original justice, the defect of the gifts of intellect and will with which Adam and Eve were adorned before the fall. Third: propensity or inclination to evil. We not only lack the original justice that inclined us to good; when it was removed a contrary quality opposed to the law took its place and makes us prone to every baseness.

3. The first part is propagated neither through soul nor through body as such, but through natural generation — as lineage, nobility, and hereditary right are. Charles is heir because he is the king's son, and the king's son because the king begot him; he is noble because he descends by natural generation from noble parents. So Adam's sin is ours because we are his sons and heirs by natural generation from him. This coincides with those who say a God-created soul becomes corrupt and guilty through hypostatic union with the body: from that union comes the whole human who is Adam's successor and so guilty of Adam's disobedience.

4. Note three points carefully. First: this concerns only a successor begotten by natural generation — by the ordinary concurrence of male and female. Otherwise our Lord Jesus Christ would be guilty of Adam's sin, which is absurd and impious. Second: the blessed Virgin is necessarily guilty of Adam's sin. What makes us guilty of it is found in her; she descends from Adam as we do; therefore she is no less guilty than we.

5. Third: only the first human's sins pass to children, not later parents' sins. The first human received justice not for himself alone but for all his posterity: if he remained in it he would transmit it with nature; if he forsook it by sinning he would pour the stain with nature into all posterity. Later parents were not instituted under that law, so their sins — like their justice — are not propagated but remain singular and personal.

6. Parents transmit the second part — lack of original justice — negatively, as poor and ignoble parents transmit want and obscure lineage: children lack goods their parents cannot confer. So a newborn lacks original justice because the parents lack it and cannot communicate it. Why then do not faithful parents, somewhat restored by grace, transfuse those gifts? Because transmitting this gift to descendants was granted only to the first parents before the fall — not to later parents, nor even to Adam after he once sinned.

7. The third part is commonly said to be transmitted as leprosy is — through seed. Infection in a leper's seed is not leprosy formally and actually but only virtually, a hidden disposition toward leprosy. So spiritual infection in the seed is not sin actually and formally but a hidden disposition toward sin; thus a soul God creates in the body contracts vice from the body from the first, as in a foul place. The solid ground is the natural mutual sympathy — communication of passions and affections — between body and soul as substantial parts of one natural composite. When the body is badly affected, the soul is badly affected.

source_text:
ART. VII.
Solvuntur argumenta quae afferri solent contra praecedentem doctrinam de propagatione nativae corruptionis per semen parentum.

1. Objicitur primo sic: corpus non potest agere in spiritum, vitiosam aliquam qualitatem ei imprimendo: Ergo concupiscentia seu propensio ad malum a corpore ad animam non derivatur. Respondet ex Augustino Pareus, lib. 4. de amissione gratiae, cap. 12., non omnino fieri naturaliter, sed occulto DEI judicio, quod anima a carne vitiata, ob culpam primorum parentum, vitium contrahat; i.e. licet corpus in spiritum naturaliter agere nequeat, per occultam tamen justitiam divinae legis illud fieri posse. 2. Alii respondent, id non fieri per actionem carnis in animam, sed per quandam naturalem concomitantiam & communicationem quae est inter materiam & formam; sicut enim anima corpori communicat suas affectiones, ut vitam, sensum, & alia hujusmodi, ita etiam dispositiones corporis communicantur animae; nam anima infusa corpori male disposito fit stolida, ut videre est in naturaliter fatuis; ita sentit Esthius Theol. Pontif. lib. 2. sent. 35. art. 1. 3. Tertio, Hieron. Zanchius, de operibus DEI parte 3. lib. 2. cap. 5., respondet animam ex conjunctione cum corpore peccato infici, non per Physicam actionem corporis in animam, sed ex justissima DEI ordinatione, qui sic initio constituerat, ut sicut si Adam non peccasset, tota illius justitia in liberos propagaretur, sic illo peccante tota naturae corruptio, quae ejus inobedientiam est consecuta, ab illo tanquam a capite in omnes homines flueret & derivaretur, idque per semen tanquam vehiculum quo ista labes a parente ad prolem transfertur.

2. Quarto, Alensis & Bonaventura in 2 Sent. dicunt animam in corpore immundo vitiari, non quod caro spiritum inficiat vera & reali actione, sed quod caro destituta originali rectitudine ac rebellis rationi effecta animum deorsum trahat, ac per hoc obliquam & distortam efficiat. Hanc sententiam explicans Pareus dicit nos posse imaginari corpus, licet brutum sit, ad mala pronum esse, & non aptum animae ad bonas actiones organum: animam vero rectitudine & puritate originali orbatam sequi inclinationem & vitiosum temperamentum corporis: idem etiam innuit clariss. Hommius in suo Antibellarmino, disput. 58. Thes. 5.

3. Secundo objicitur: Si DEUS animam puram in carcerem tam impurum detrudit, crudeliter ac injuste agit: at impium & blasphemum est posterius; Ergo & prius est absurdum. Resp. concedendo totum; nos enim non dicimus DEUM immittere animam justam & puram in corpus impurum; inde enim sequitur animas nostras esse justas ante earum infusionem & conjunctionem cum corporibus, quod postea refutabitur art. 8. Instabit aliquis: DEUS infundit animam, ex se peccatum non habentem, corpori impuro & contagioso: Ergo injuste agit. Resp. negando consequentiam; is enim agit injuste qui illud agit cujus contrarium agere tenetur ex aequo & bono; sed DEUS non tenetur animas filiorum Adae, qui in Adamo peccaverunt & sic aeternam mortem meriti sunt, puris corporibus infundere; h.e. non tenetur corpora nostra, labe peccati foedata, ante infusionem animarum purgare; sed contra, tenetur ea non purgare, idque vi illius comminationis, Quo die comederis, moriendo morieris.

4. Tertio obj.: causa causae est etiam causa causati: at DEUS est causa unionis animae cum corpore; anima ex conjunctione cum corpore contrahit peccatum; nam unio est causa illius peccati in anima: Ergo DEUS est causa peccati. Respondet Zanchius, unionem animae cum corpore non per se, sed per accidens esse causam peccati, idque quia si Adam non peccasset, DEUS copulasset animas cum corporibus sine ulla peccati consecutione: quare ex accidente est quod nunc animae labes eam conjunctionem consequatur. 2. Respond. DEUM tantum creare animas in corpore, parentes vero per virtutem prolificam animas substantialiter cum corporibus conjungere: quare quod animas habeamus in corporibus nostris, est a DEO; quod vero animas habeamus in corporibus impuris & contagiosis creatas, est a lapsu primorum parentum. In summa, illa regula, causa causae est causa causati, intelligenda est de causis per se, non per accidens. DEUS enim est causa suae legis, & lex divina est causa peccati per accidens, ut patet ex cap. 7. ad Rom. a vers. 8. ad 14.; nemo tamen inde concludere potest DEUM esse peccati causam.

5. Quarto obj.: quod corpus non habet, eo non potest animam inficere; at peccatum, quod animae est proprium, nimirum ignorantia mentis & aversio voluntatis a bono, non inest corpori: Ergo corpus peccato animam inficere non potest. Resp. sicut semen parentis leprosi producit lepram in corporibus filiorum, licet actu & formaliter in se non habeat lepram, sed occultam quandam dispositionem ad lepram, ita etiam caro potest inficere animam peccato, licet actu & formaliter in se non habeat peccatum, sed tantum dispositionem virtualem ad peccatum. Respondetur igitur ad propositionem: quod corpus in se habet nullo modo, h.e. neque formaliter neque virtualiter, eo non potest inficere animam; potest tamen virtualiter habere quod formaliter non habet.

6. Quinto obj.: in Adamo peccatum primo fuit in anima, quam in carne, & ab anima in carnem, non a carne ad animam transit: Ergo eodem ordine in filiis Adae vitium existit; anima enim, non corpus, est πρωτοπαθὲς peccati. Respondet Pareus, alium fuisse ordinem in vitii operatione quae a libero arbitrio cepit; alium esse in vitii generatione quae a carne procedit. Responderi etiam potest eundem ordinem adhuc servari, & animam etiam nunc esse πρωτοπαθὲς peccati, idque quia ignorantia, contumacia, & aversio a bono actu & formaliter primo inest animae, deinde corpori; licet dispositive & virtualiter insint corpori prius quam animae. Hic nobis se offert occasio reprehendendi crassam & absurdam eorum sententiam, qui dicunt peccatum originis actu & formaliter in semine inesse ante adventum animae. Primo enim habitus & privatio versantur circa idem: Ergo privatio non potest esse in subjecto in quo habitus inesse non potest; atqui in semine non potest esse justitia originalis, quae est habitus: ergo neque in eo existere potest peccatum originale, quod est ejus privatio. Secundo, si semen actu & formaliter in se peccatum habet, varia sequentur absurda. Primo, semini datam esse legem, lex enim, inquit Paulus, data est peccatoribus; secundo, semen esse obnoxium aeternae damnationi, quod enim proprie peccatum in se habet, id damnari in aeternum potest; tertio, semen posse a CHRISTO redimi, salvari, poenitentiam agere, & credere, quae omnia tam absurda sunt, inquit Keckermannus, ut cogitari vix absurdus possit.
english: Article VII. Objections against native corruption's propagation through parental seed are answered.

1. First objection: a body cannot act on a spirit by impressing a vicious quality; so concupiscence is not derived from body to soul. Pareus (from Augustine) answers that the soul contracts vice from vitiated flesh not wholly by nature but by God's hidden judgment for the first parents' fault — the body cannot naturally act on spirit, yet by the hidden justice of the divine law it can happen. Others locate it not in flesh's action on soul but in natural concomitance between matter and form: as the soul communicates life and sense to the body, so the body's dispositions are communicated to the soul (a soul infused into a badly disposed body becomes dull, as in the naturally foolish — Esthius). Zanchi adds: infection comes from conjunction with the body not by physical action but by God's just ordinance — as Adam's justice would have flowed to children if he had not sinned, so when he sinned nature's corruption flows from him as head into all, through seed as the vehicle of the stain.

2. Alexander of Hales and Bonaventure: the soul is vitiated in an unclean body not by flesh truly acting on spirit, but because flesh stripped of original rectitude and rebellious to reason draws the mind down and warps it. Pareus: imagine the body prone to evils and unfit as an organ for good acts; the soul, robbed of original purity, follows that vicious temperament (Hommius likewise).

3. Second objection: if God thrusts a pure soul into so impure a prison he acts cruelly — which is blasphemous to say, so the premise is absurd. We concede the whole: we do not say God sends a just, pure soul into an impure body (that would make souls just before infusion — refuted in Art. VIII). Press: God infuses a soul that of itself has no sin into a contagious body, so he acts unjustly. Deny the consequence. Injustice is doing what equity binds one to do the contrary of. God is not bound to give Adam's children — who sinned in Adam and merited eternal death — pure bodies before infusion; by the threat In the day you eat you shall die he is bound not to purge them.

4. Third: the cause of a cause is cause of the caused; God causes union; union causes the soul's sin; so God causes sin. Zanchi: union is a cause of sin only per accidens — had Adam not sinned, God would have joined souls and bodies without sin following. Further: God creates souls in the body; parents by prolific virtue substantially unite them. Having souls in bodies is from God; having them created in impure bodies is from the fall. The rule applies to causes per se, not per accidens. God causes his law; the law causes sin per accidens (Rom 7:8–14); yet God is not the cause of sin.

5. Fourth: what the body lacks it cannot use to infect the soul; but soul-proper sin (ignorance, aversion from good) is not in the body. Answer: as leprous seed produces leprosy without having leprosy formally — only a hidden disposition — so flesh can infect the soul with only a virtual disposition toward sin. What the body has neither formally nor virtually cannot infect; what it has virtually can.

6. Fifth: in Adam sin was first in the soul and passed to flesh, not reverse; so in his children the soul is first-sufferer. Pareus: the order in vice from free choice differs from the order in vice generated from flesh. Or: the soul is still first-sufferer actually and formally, though the body has the disposition virtually first. Those who put original sin actually and formally in the seed before the soul are absurd: habit and privation concern the same subject; original justice cannot be in seed, so neither can its privation. If seed had sin formally, seed would have a law, face eternal damnation, and be able to be redeemed, repent, and believe — absurdities Keckermann says can scarcely be outdone.

source_text:
ART. VIII.
Proponuntur & solvuntur aliquot quaestiones de propagatione peccati originalis.

1. Prima quaestio est, quomodo possit peccatum originale traduci & propagari, cum anima, quae illius subjectum est, non traducatur; non potest enim accidens traduci sine subjecto? Respondet Doctor Esthius, accidentia frequenter traduci, id est, affectione quadam vel infectione transire in alterum, non transeunte subjecto; nam haereses, errores, vitia ab uno in multos propagantur non transeunte eorum subjecto, hoc est, anima; quae quidem responsio vera & solida est, si intelligatur de ea traductione qua accidens non idem numero, sed idem specie, transit & traducitur ab uno in aliud; cum enim traducitur idem numero accidens, necesse est etiam ejus subjectum traduci & transire. Sic, ut putant nonnulli Philosophi, odore transeunte in manum hominis contrectantis, transeunt etiam subtiliores partes pomi, in quibus odor proxime existit.

2. Secunda quaestio: An anima peccaverit in lumbis Adae? Distinguendum est: anima potest considerari vel quoad esse simpliciter, vel quoad esse in corpore & unionem cum corpore. Priori modo considerata anima non potest dici fuisse in lumbis Adae, & per consequens non potest dici peccasse in lumbis Adae; posteriori vero modo considerata bene dici potest ab Adamo extrahi, in lumbis ejus fuisse, & peccasse; totus enim homo fuit in lumbis Adae, idque quia ab Adamo descendit per naturalem generationem, & proinde totus homo est reus peccati ab Adamo admissi; totus autem homo ad poenam obligari nequit, nisi & anima & corpus ejus ad poenam obligentur.

3. Tertia quaestio: An DEUS creando & infundendo animam, peccatum originale in eam imprimat? Respondemus negative. DEUS creando animam non confert ei puritatem seu justitiam & sanctitatem, neque impuritatem & propensionem ad malum, sed tantum essentiam spiritualem & proprietates ab essentia dimanantes: dico DEUM non inspirare animae venenum lethale concupiscentiae, quia mali author esse non vult: dico etiam eum non infundere animae sanctitatem & justitiam, quia anima creatur ut sit pars constitutiva filii & successoris Adami, cui DEUS spiritualia dona conferre non tenetur; vide clarissimi Junii Comment. in Cap. 2. Genes.
english: Article VIII. Several questions on the propagation of original sin are proposed and answered.

1. First: how can original sin be translated when its subject, the soul, is not? Esthius: accidents often pass by affection or infection without the subject's passing — as heresies, errors, and vices spread from one to many without the soul's passing. That holds for an accident the same in species, not in number; a numerically identical accident requires its subject's transfer too. Some philosophers similarly say that when odor passes into a handling hand, the fruit's subtler parts that proximately bear the odor also pass.

2. Second: Did the soul sin in Adam's loins? Distinguish. As to being simply, the soul was not in Adam's loins and did not sin there. As to being in the body and union with it, it can be said to be drawn from Adam, to have been in his loins, and to have sinned: the whole human was in Adam's loins by natural generation and so is guilty of Adam's sin; the whole human is not bound to punishment unless both soul and body are.

3. Third: Does God impress original sin by creating and infusing the soul? No. In creating the soul God confers neither justice and holiness nor impurity and propensity to evil, but only a spiritual essence and properties that flow from it. He does not breathe the lethal poison of concupiscence — he will not be evil's author — nor does he infuse holiness and justice, for the soul is created as a constitutive part of Adam's son and successor, to whom God is not bound to give spiritual gifts (Junius on Gen 2).

source_text:
ART. IX.
Diluuntur leviora argumenta quae afferri solent contra creationem & infusionem animae.

1. Objicitur primo: DEUS sex primis diebus totum creationis opus absolvit, postea vero requievit ab opere suo, Gen. 2, Exod. 20; non igitur novae animae nunc creantur. Respond. DEUM post sextum diem cessasse a creatione novarum specierum, non vero novorum individuorum: animae autem, quas jam creat, non specie sed numero differunt ab anima Adami, quam primo creavit.

2. Secundo obj.: Genes. 5 dicitur Adam genuisse filium ad imaginem suam; est autem filius imago & similitudo patris secundum animam: Ergo Adam genuit filium secundum animam. Resp. filium esse imaginem & similitudinem patris non tam ratione animae quam ratione totius suppositi, i.e. quatenus est quid constans ex anima & corpore: Adam ergo non solum genuit filium similem patri, ut vult Esthius, sed etiam genuit id in quo illa similitudo potissimum consistit, videlicet ipsam personam filii sui, ex anima & corpore conflatam.

3. Tertio obj.: Genes. 46 dicuntur 70 animae egressae de femore Iacobi, quod non est aliud quam feminis propagatione traduci. Respond. animas synecdochice pro hominibus esse positas: addere etiam possumus, ipsas animas egressas fuisse ex femore Iacobi, non quod e femore Iacobi traductae sint quoad earum esse simpliciter, sed quod ex eo descenderint quoad earum existentiam in corpore & unionem cum corpore; virtus enim seminis egressi ex femore Iacobi effecit unionem corporis & animae.

4. Quarto obj.: si homo generando non producit animam rationalem, pejoris est conditionis quam bruta & plantae, quae producunt animas sibi proprias, videlicet vegetativam & sensitivam. Respondet Esthius, hominem esse melioris conditionis etiam in officio generandi quam sunt bruta aut plantae, eo quod vis ejus generativa pertingat ad unionem nobilissimae formae cum materia, ut supra declaratum est. Adde quod hoc ipsum ad magnam dignitatem pertinet, talem habere animam, ad quam producendam, propter ipsius excellentiam, nulla vis naturae possit pertingere; qua ratione nec angelis, quorum natura excellentior est quam hominum, vis ulla generandi competit.

5. Quinto obj.: si homo non generat animam filii sed corpus, non generat totum hominem, sed alteram ejus partem, imo ignobiliorem ejus partem. Resp. negando sequelam: Maria enim non genuit Deitatem CHRISTI, & tamen vere dicitur genuisse totum CHRISTUM: ignis etiam, cum ex ligno generat alium ignem, non generat materiam illius ignis, sed tantum formam, & tamen dicitur generare seu producere totum illum ignem; secundum definitionem Aristotelis, generatio est mutatio totius, &c. Quare hic distinguendum est inter totum hominem & totum hominis; pater enim generat totum hominem, id est, omnes partes.

6. Sexto obj.: si DEUS sigillatim creat animas omnium qui quomodocunque gignuntur, cooperatur scortatoribus & adulteris: nam fornicariis & adulterinis conceptibus animas creat & largitur, quod videtur absurdum. Resp. DEUS cooperatur generationi naturali, quae est per se bona & opus naturae; non autem vitio quo fornicatores & adulteri contra legem DEI generationem perficiunt.
english: Article IX. Lighter arguments against the creation and infusion of the soul are dissolved.

1. Objection: God finished creation in six days and rested (Gen 2; Exod 20), so new souls are not now created. Answer: after the sixth day he ceased creating new species, not new individuals. Souls he now creates differ from Adam's first-created soul in number, not in species.

2. Genesis 5: Adam begot a son in his image; a son is the father's image according to the soul; so Adam begot according to the soul. Answer: the likeness is chiefly of the whole person consisting of soul and body, not of the soul alone. Adam begot not only a like son but the very person composed of soul and body in which that likeness chiefly consists (Esthius).

3. Genesis 46: seventy souls went out from Jacob's thigh — supposedly translation by seed. Answer: souls stand synecdochically for humans. Or: souls went out from Jacob's thigh not as to simple being but as to existence in the body and union with it; the seed's virtue effected that union.

4. If generating does not produce a rational soul, humans are worse off than brutes and plants that produce their own vegetative and sensitive souls. Esthius: humans are better off even in generating, because generative power reaches the union of the noblest form with matter. It is dignity to have a soul so excellent that no natural power can produce it — which is why even angels have no generative power.

5. If the father generates only the body, he does not generate the whole human but the less noble part. Deny the sequel. Mary did not beget Christ's deity yet truly begot the whole Christ; fire from wood generates fire's form, not its matter, yet generates that whole fire (Aristotle: generation is change of the whole). Distinguish the whole human from the whole of the human: the father generates the whole human — all the parts.

6. If God creates each soul of whoever is begotten, he cooperates with fornicators and adulterers. Answer: God cooperates with natural generation, good of itself and nature's work — not with the vice by which they complete generation against his law.

source_text:
ART. X.
An possit reddi commodior aliqua, aut expeditior ratio traductionis concupiscentiae, seu propensionis ad malum, quam diximus esse tertiam partem peccati originalis.

1. Qui communem sententiam de infectione animae a corpore ad peccandum disposito spernunt & rejiciunt, illi ad quatuor classes seu ordines vocari & reduci possunt. Primo enim, Traduciarii, qui animarum creationem impugnant, firmissime asseverant se ex suae sententiae fundamentis posse reddere longe meliorem & tutiorem rationem traductionis peccati quam nos, qui animarum creationem defendimus: de his postea.

2. Secundo, sunt qui dicunt hominem naturaliter constare ex carne & spiritu, & ideo partim cum bestiis, partim cum Angelis communicare naturam: & quidem ratione carnis & communionis cum bestiis, habere propensionem quandam ad bonum corporale & sensibile, in quod fertur per sensum & appetitum; ratione spiritus & communionis cum Angelis, habere propensionem ad bonum spirituale & intelligibile, in quod fertur per intellectum & voluntatem. Ex his autem diversis vel contrariis propensionibus in uno eodemque homine naturaliter seu per necessariam consecutionem ex principiis essentialibus, existere volunt pugnam quandam inter sensum & rationem, & ex ea pugna ingentem bene agendi difficultatem, dum una propensio alteram impedit.

3. Dicunt secundo, divinam providentiam, initio creationis, ut remedium adhiberet huic morboso languori naturae humanae, qui ex conditione principiorum essentialium oriebatur, addidisse homini donum quoddam insigne, justitiam videlicet originalem, qua veluti aureo quodam freno appetitus sensitivus contineretur & rationi subjiceretur.

4. Dicunt tertio, post lapsum Adamum amisisse illud donum originale, & proinde nunc in nobis concupiscentiam seu propensionem ad malum dimanare ex ipsa animae constitutione essentiali, qua constituitur ex parte sensitiva & parte rationali; partim ex carentia originalis justitiae, quae partem sensitivam parti intellectivae subjiciebat.

5. Haec doctrina merito rejicitur a nostris Theologis. Primo, quia est fundamentum absurdi illius dogmatis de concupiscentia in renatis, quod videlicet post baptismum non sit peccatum, sed morbus & languor quidam naturae. Secundo, quia falso asserit rebellionem appetitus sensitivi contra rationem & ejus directionem esse naturalem: nam illi qui hoc asserunt DEO contumeliosi sunt, dicentes DEUM illum sanctissimum, qui peccatum odit & exsecratur, ipsi naturae humanae in prima creatione indidisse impetum tam rebellem & iniquum, videlicet propensionem ad peccandum, & talia ac inhonesta objecta appetendum. Tertio, quia (fatente Bellarmino ipso, lib. 5. de amissione gratiae) vitiosa illa concupiscentia non solum est in appetitu sensitivo qui rationi resistit, sed etiam in voluntate quae prona est ad concupiscendos honores, inanem gloriam, & appetendum illa objecta quae sensui jucunda sunt & rationi displicent, cum prius contrario modo se habuerit, idque naturaliter. Hic haeret Bellarminus, & aeternum haerebit, donec nostram sententiam de concupiscentia in renatis amplexus fuerit.

6. Bellarminus ad secundam rationem a nobis jam allatam respondens, lib. de gratia primi hominis cap. 7., concupiscentiam (inquit) carnis fuisse homini in primo statu naturalem, non quidem ut bonum aliquod naturae, sed ut defectum & quasi morbum quendam naturae ex materiae conditione consequentem. Quare rectissime dicitur concupiscentiam non esse ex DEO, odio non amore dignam, malam, naturaeque contrariam, propter duas causas: primum quia non ex intentione authoris naturae sed praeter ejus intentionem in homine extitisset, si in puris naturalibus homo creatus fuisset; deinde quia DEUS illam sustulerat, & ex ipsius hominis culpa locum in nobis habet.

7. Haec doctrina Bellarmini nimis crassa & absurda est. Primo, quia dicit hanc rebellionem esse a natura, & tamen non esse a DEO, qui fons est & causa naturae — manifestam contradictionem implicat. Secundo, quia DEUS non potest producere aliquid suae naturae contrarium; natura enim DEI sicut est ipsa bonitas, ita est ipsa propensio ad bonum, & proinde contrariatur propensioni ad malum. Tertio, donum illud supernaturale justitiae, ex sententia Bellarmini, non sustulit naturalem propensionem appetitus sensitivi ad concupiscendum contra ordinem rationis — sic enim ipsam naturam appetitus sensitivi evertisset — sed tantum eam cohibuit ne actu resisteret rationi & aliquid appeteret contra rationis directionem: Ergo Adamus in statu integritatis habuit in appetitu suo propensionem ad malum, quamvis nondum erupisset in actus & exercitia istius propensionis, & per consequens originali peccato inquinatus fuit; quid enim aliud est peccatum originale, quam propensio ad malum?
english: Article X. Whether a more convenient account of the traduction of concupiscence can be given than we gave as original sin's third part.

1. Those who reject the common view — that the soul is infected from a body disposed to sin — fall into four classes. First: Traducians, who attack soul-creation and claim their foundations yield a far safer account of sin's traduction than ours. Of them later.

2. Second class: they say a human naturally consists of flesh and spirit, sharing nature with beasts and with angels. By flesh he has a propensity to corporal, sensible good via sense and appetite; by spirit, to spiritual, intelligible good via intellect and will. From these contrary propensities, flowing necessarily from essential principles, they posit a fight between sense and reason and from it a huge difficulty of acting well.
3. Second, they say providence at creation added original justice as a golden bridle to remedy that diseased languor arising from the essential principles, holding sensitive appetite under reason.

4. Third, after the fall Adam lost that gift; so now concupiscence flows partly from the soul's essential constitution (sensitive and rational parts) and partly from lack of the original justice that subjected sense to intellect.

5. Our theologians rightly reject this. First: it underwrites the absurd dogma that concupiscence in the regenerate after baptism is not sin but a natural disease. Second: calling the sensitive appetite's rebellion natural insults God — as if the most holy God who hates sin impressed on human nature at creation a propensity to sin and to dishonest objects. Third: Bellarmine himself admits (Loss of Grace 5) that vicious concupiscence is also in the will, prone to honors, empty glory, and objects pleasant to sense and displeasing to reason — though it once held the contrary naturally. Here Bellarmine sticks until he takes our view of concupiscence in the regenerate.

6. Answering us (Grace of the First Human 7), Bellarmine says fleshly concupiscence was natural in the first state not as a good of nature but as a defect or disease following from matter's condition. So it is rightly called not from God, hate-worthy, evil, contrary to nature: it would have existed beside the author's intention if humans were created in pure naturals; and God had removed it, and by human fault it has place in us.

7. Crass and absurd. First: rebellion from nature yet not from God, nature's fount, is a contradiction. Second: God cannot produce what is contrary to his nature — goodness itself and propensity to good, contrary to propensity to evil. Third: on Bellarmine's view the supernatural gift of justice did not remove the sensitive appetite's natural propensity against reason's order (that would overturn its nature) but only restrained actual resistance. So Adam in integrity already had a propensity to evil in his appetite, though not yet broken into acts — and so was stained with original sin. What else is original sin than propensity to evil?

source_text:
ART. XI.
Considerantur duae aliae sententiae de traductione peccati.

1. Sequuntur in hoc articulo considerandae tertia & quarta classes eorum qui communem sententiam de infectione animae a corpore rejiciunt. Ad tertiam classem eos refero, qui dicunt peccatum originale traduci a parentibus ad liberos per solam generationem naturalem, absque ulla infectione animae a corpore: generationem (inquiunt) esse quidem causam cur nos rei sumus peccati ab Adamo commissi; non vero posse esse causam nostrae caecitatis, ignorantiae, & propensionis ad malum; & proinde haec opinio in eo peccat, quod secundum eam explicari possit traductio primae partis peccati originalis, non vero secundae & tertiae partis.

2. Ad quartam classem eos refero, qui nobiscum consentiunt in explicanda traductione primae & secundae partis peccati originalis, dissentiunt vero in explicanda traductione tertiae partis; dicentes eam propagari & traduci a parentibus ad liberos, non per se, sed per secundam partem; h.e. per carentiam originalis justitiae, cum qua necessario connexa & conjuncta est. Si quis igitur eos roget, undenam sit quod infans recens natus sit reus peccati ab Adamo commissi? Respondebunt, quia est filius Adami, h.e. quia ab eo per naturalem generationem descendit. Item si roget, unde caret originali justitia? Respondebunt, quia parentes ea carent & eam conferre nequeunt. Si vero roget, unde propensio ad malum? Dicent eam necessario consequi carentiam justitiae originalis, tanquam tenebras carentiam luminis.

3. Verum haec sententia non satisfacit. Primo, quia carentia justitiae originalis est mera privatio & non Ens; at non Ens non potest esse causa Entis realis, qualis est propensio ad malum, quae habitum quendam positivum & realem importat, ut docet ipse Molinaeus cap. 8. istius operis: Ergo carentia justitiae non habet realem & positivam causalitatem ad producendam concupiscentiam. Dicet aliquis: caecitas, quae est privatio, potest esse causa lapsus, & privatio luminis potest esse causa aberrationis a via; lapsus autem & aberratio a via sunt entia realia. Resp. lapsus & aberratio non producuntur a privatione tanquam a causa efficiente positiva, sed privatio est conditio sine qua non, seu causa per accidens.

4. Secundo, proposita sunt nonnulla asserta Molinaei de intellectu hominis justitia originali destituti, idque in eorum gratiam qui nondum Molinaeum legerunt. Prima assertio: Intellectus hominis originali justitia destituti, & nondum per verbi praedicationem vocati, neque cognoscit, neque cognoscere potest, durante eo statu, bona spiritualia & supernaturalia. Haec assertio probatione non eget; nam ut docet Bellarminus lib. 6. de gratia & libero arbitrio cap. 1., convenit inter omnes Theologos, sive sint Pontificii sive Evangelici, ista mysteria fidei sine divina revelatione cognosci non posse.

5. Secunda assertio Molinaei non probat concupiscentiam oriri mere ex carentia justitiae. Tertio, concupiscentia seu propensio ad malum non solum est pronitas ad nimium amorem rerum terrenarum, orta ex ignorantia rerum caelestium & supernaturalium (ut statuit haec sententia); sed etiam est pronitas quaedam ad contemnenda & negligenda bona illa caelestia quae nobis patefacta & revelata sunt, h.e. quorum cognitionem ex verbi auditu acquisivimus; item est propensio ad ea agenda quorum turpitudinem ex DEI verbo cognitam & perspectam habemus. Unde Paulus de seipso conqueritur, Rom. 7:22–23: Delector (inquit) lege DEI secundum interiorem hominem; sed video aliam legem in membris meis rebellantem legi mentis meae, & captivum me ducentem in lege peccati quae est in membris meis.

6. Quarto, si concupiscentia carnis nihil aliud sit nisi propensio ad inordinatum amorem rerum terrenarum, orta ex ignorantia rerum caelestium, absurdum sequetur dogma: videlicet concupiscentiam post illuminationem verbi & regenerationem non manere; at experientia & Scriptura docent eam manere in renatis. Quare sententia quae tertiam partem peccati originalis sola carentia justitiae explicat, rejicienda est.
english: Article XI. Two other opinions on the traduction of sin are considered.

1. Next are the third and fourth classes that reject the common view of the soul's infection from the body. Third class: original sin is translated by natural generation alone, without infection of soul from body. Generation explains why we are guilty of Adam's sin, they say, but not our blindness, ignorance, and propensity to evil. So this view can account for the first part of original sin, not the second and third.

2. Fourth class: they agree with us on the first and second parts, but say the third is propagated not through itself but through the second — lack of original justice, to which it is necessarily joined. Why is a newborn guilty of Adam's sin? Because he is Adam's son by natural generation. Why does he lack original justice? Because parents lack it and cannot confer it. Whence propensity to evil? It necessarily follows lack of justice, as darkness follows lack of light.

3. This does not satisfy. Lack of original justice is mere privation and non-being; non-being cannot cause a real being such as propensity to evil, which imports a positive real habit (Molinaeus ch. 8). So lack of justice has no real positive causality for producing concupiscence. Objection: blindness causes a fall; lack of light causes wandering — and those are real. Answer: privation is not a positive efficient cause but a condition sine qua non, or a cause per accidens.

4. For readers who have not met Molinaeus: his first assertion — that the intellect destitute of original justice and not yet called by the word neither knows nor can know spiritual and supernatural goods while that state lasts — needs no proof. Bellarmine (Grace and Free Choice 6.1): all theologians, Pontifical and Evangelical, agree those mysteries of faith cannot be known without divine revelation.

5. His further claims do not prove concupiscence arises merely from lack of justice. Concupiscence is not only proneness to excessive love of earthly things from ignorance of heavenly ones; it is also proneness to despising revealed heavenly goods known from the word, and to doing what we know from God's word to be base. So Paul (Rom 7:22–23): I delight in God's law in the inner human, but see another law in my members rebelling and leading me captive under sin's law.

6. If fleshly concupiscence were only inordinate love of earthly things from ignorance of heavenly ones, it would not remain after the word's illumination and regeneration — yet experience and Scripture say it remains in the regenerate. So explaining the third part by mere lack of justice is to be rejected.

source_text:
ART. XII.
Ostenditur eos qui animarum creationem impugnant multum inter se dissentire; & confutantur tres primae eorum sententiae de origine animae.

1. Statueram apud me, in hac Exercitatione, postquam communem sententiam de origine animae & propagatione peccati proposuissem & defendissem, etiam adversariorum sententias de traduce propositae & confutatae essent, idque in eorum gratiam qui nondum Molinaeum legerunt. Et nihilominus serio damnare & rejicere dogma illud de eductione animae rationalis ex potentia materiae ideo operae pretium me facturum sentiebam, si proponerem & sigillatim confutarem omnes sententias quas memini me legisse aut audivisse de traductione animarum.

2. Prima sententia est Jacobi Martini, qui in lib. 3. Miscellanearum quaestionum, disput. 7., dicit animam filii esse ab anima patris per traducem, modo tamen impervestigabili & nobis incognito. Hic modus recedendi a communi sententia facilis est, sed inhonestus, & si quid judico, tanti viri acumine indignus: verum ne illi qui his latebris se occultant secure delitescant, contra eos utar unico argumento, sed nisi me animus fallit, valido & perspicuo; illud autem sic proponi potest: Quod a nulla causa naturaliter & per se producitur, nisi modo aliquo nobis cognito, id non potest dici a causa naturali produci modo nobis incognito: at anima rationalis a nulla causa naturali producitur modo nobis cognito: Ergo neque modo nobis incognito. Qui enim latibulum ignorantiae quaerit, cum causas physicas assignare nequit, is sententiam suam non firmat sed destruit.

3. Secunda sententia est eorum qui dicunt animam educi ex potentia seminis — quam sententiam Meisnerus acerrime propugnat, non immerito rejicitur. Argumenta ejus haec sunt: 1. Accidens, videlicet virtus seminalis, non potest producere tam nobilem & excellentem substantiam. 2. Anima est forma immaterialis: Ergo non est in semine ante adventum animae. 3. Formarum materialium proprium est educi e potentia materiae; anima autem est forma spiritualis. Vide caetera apud ipsum Meisnerum, loco citato. Haec argumenta, ut contra eductionem ex potentia materiae valent, ita etiam ostendunt animam non esse ex traduce materiali.

4. Tertia sententia est eorum qui affirmant parentem simul cum semine emittere suae animae particulam, & proinde semen primo cum emittitur esse actu animatum; hi igitur volunt animam filii esse ab anima patris per ejus divisionem & quasi imminutionem. Hunc modum tuendi animarum traducem non satis tutum judicat Meisnerus, & merito; quia ex eo sequitur animam divisibilem & proinde materialem & corruptibilem esse; quia quod dividitur & imminuitur, quantum & materiale est.
english: Article XII. Those who attack the creation of souls disagree among themselves; three of their opinions on the soul's origin are refuted.

1. After defending the common view on the soul's origin and sin's propagation, I meant also to propose and confute the adversaries' traducian opinions — for readers who have not yet met Molinaeus. Because I seriously reject eduction of the rational soul from matter's potency, it seemed worthwhile to confute one by one every opinion on soul-traduction I remember reading or hearing.

2. First: Jacob Martini (Miscellanies 3.7) — the child's soul is from the father's by a translate in an uninvestigable, unknown way. Easy, but dishonest, and unworthy of so sharp a man. Against those who hide in that den: what no natural cause produces per se in any way known to us cannot be said to be produced by a natural cause in an unknown way; but no natural cause produces the rational soul in a known way; therefore not in an unknown way either. Seeking ignorance's hiding-place when physical causes cannot be assigned destroys the opinion rather than strengthens it.

3. Second: those who say the soul is educed from the seed's potency — which Meisner keenly defends and which is rightly rejected. His own arguments: an accident (seminal virtue) cannot produce so noble a substance; the soul is an immaterial form, so not in the seed before arrival; material forms are educed from matter's potency, but the soul is spiritual. As these strike eduction from matter, they also strike a material translate.

4. Third: the parent emits with the seed a particle of his soul, so the seed is actually animated when emitted; the child's soul comes by division and a kind of diminution of the father's. Meisner rightly judges this unsafe: it makes the soul divisible and therefore material and corruptible — for what is divided and diminished is quantitative and material.

source_text:
ART. XIII.
Refellitur quarta sententia, quae est Balthasaris Meisneri.

1. Quarta sententia, quam amplectitur Balthasar Meisnerus, in hoc convenit cum praecedente, quod statuat animam non e potentia seminis educi, sed a parente in prolem traduci, & una cum semine in matricem infundi; ac proinde semen quamprimum emittitur, esse actu animatum: differt tamen ab ea, quatenus asserit animam illam in semine existentem non fieri ex anima patris per decisionem & partitionem animae paternae, sed ab ea generari & produci de novo. Hanc sententiam explicans Meisnerus pag. 924. sic ait: quamprimum parens semen transfundit in uterum genitricis, unc una cum semine transmittit animam, non quidem suam aut suae partem, sed suae similem.

2. Quatuor sunt modi quibus aliquid fieri dicitur ex aliquo. 1. Fit aliquid ex aliquo effective, ut effectus a causa efficiente. 2. Fit aliquid ex aliquo materialiter, quomodo dicimus exiguum clavum fieri ex ingenti massa ferri, & exiguum annulum ex ingenti massa auri. 3. Fit aliquid ex aliquo subjective, illud videlicet quod ex alicujus subjecti potentia educitur, quomodo dicimus omnes formas materiales fieri & educi ex potentia materiae. 4. Fit aliquid ex aliquo constitutive, quomodo dicimus omnia corpora naturalia fieri ex materia & forma.

3. His positis, sic probatur animam patris creare animam filii ex Meisneri sententia: Quod producit aliquid ex nihilo, illud creat: at anima patris producit animam filii ex nihilo, ex Meisneri sententia: Ergo creat, atque proinde infinitam virtutem habet; nam producere ex nihilo seu creare infinitam virtutem arguit: propositio major est perspicua, nam nititur definitione creationis. Probatur minor: anima filii non fit ex anima patris decisive, seu per divisionem & partitionem, ut ipse Meisnerus fatetur. Tertio, non fit ex ea subjective, h.e. non educitur ex ejus potentia, quia quod educitur ex alicujus subjecti potentia, illud in eo subjecto recipitur & in eo existit; sed nemo dixerit animam filii existere in anima patris tanquam in subjecto. Quarto, anima patris non est pars constitutiva animae filii: ergo anima filii non fit ex ea constitutive. Ergo fit ex nihilo; ergo creatur ab anima patris — quod absurdum est.

4. Quod autem ad illam similitudinem a lumine petitam attinet: tenendum est eam ineptam esse, & nullo modo pro ejus sententia facere; nam lumen educitur de potentia materiae, ut omnes fatentur: unde Fonseca, 5. Metaph. cap. 2. quaest. 4. sect. 1.: Nemo (inquit) dubitat lumen educi de potentia aeris; & certe cum faci lucenti admovetur fax alia, manifestum est ex potentia materiae istius facis admotae educi flammam.

5. Praeterea, facultas procreativa similium animarum absque eductione ex potentia materiae competit animae rationali per se, & non quatenus est vegetativa — at hoc Meisnero concedi non potest sine creatione.

6. Quarto: In generatione uterque parens emittit semen, ut docent non solum Scholastici Theologi complures, lib. 3. Sent., ut Scotus, Bonaventura, Major, Occamus, Lichetus, Gabriel; sed etiam Medici multis manifestis indiciis ab Anatomica experientia ductis convincunt, quae hoc loco in medium afferre non possum; ea tamen scriptis mandarunt Galenus, Fernel, Levinus Lemnius, Vesalius, Laurentius, & multi alii. Hoc igitur posito sic argumentor: Semen utriusque parentis vel est animatum, vel alterum tantum. Si utrumque, duae animae in uno semine conflato; si alterum tantum, cur non semper generatio sequitur quando semen sufficienter dispositum emittitur?

7. Quinto: absurdum est toties verum & proprie dictum miraculum fieri, quoties pater semen sufficienter dispositum emittit & illam emissionem animatio & proinde generatio non consequitur — quod tamen sequeretur si Meisneri sententia vera esset, naturae cursu miraculose inhibito.

8. Sexto, omne rationale est homo: at semen, si actu animatum anima rationali, esset homo — absurdum ante formationem corporis.
english: Article XIII. Meisner's fourth opinion is refuted.

1. Meisner's fourth opinion agrees with the preceding that the soul is not educed from the seed's potency but translated from parent to offspring and infused with the seed into the womb, so the seed is actually animated as soon as emitted. It differs in holding that the soul in the seed is not cut off or partitioned from the father's soul but generated and produced anew by it. Meisner (p. 924): as soon as the parent transfuses seed into the mother's womb, he transmits with it a soul — not his own or a part of it, but one like his own.

2. Something can come to be from something in four ways: effectively (effect from efficient cause); materially (a small nail from a mass of iron); subjectively (educed from a subject's potency, as material forms from matter); constitutively (natural bodies from matter and form).

3. On Meisner's view the father's soul creates the child's. What produces from nothing creates; the father's soul produces the child's from nothing; so it creates and has infinite power. The child's soul is not from the father's by partition (Meisner admits); not subjectively educed from its potency (or it would exist in the father's soul as in a subject); not constitutively (the father's soul is not a constitutive part). So from nothing — creation by the father's soul — which is absurd.

4. The likeness from light is inept. Light is educed from matter's potency (Fonseca): no one doubts light is educed from air's potency; when another torch is brought to a shining one, flame is educed from the applied torch's matter.
5. A power to procreate like souls without eduction from matter would belong to the rational soul as such, not as vegetative — and that cannot be granted without creation.

6. Both parents emit seed (Scholastics on Sent. 3 — Scotus, Bonaventure, Major, Ockham, and others — and physicians from anatomy: Galen, Fernel, Lemnius, Vesalius, Laurentius). If both seeds are animated, two souls in one fused seed; if only one, why does generation not always follow when sufficiently disposed seed is emitted?

7. It is absurd that a true miracle should occur whenever a father emits sufficiently disposed seed and animation (hence generation) does not follow — yet that would follow on Meisner's view with nature's course miraculously held back.
8. Every rational thing is a human; seed actually animated by a rational soul would be a human before the body is formed — absurd.

source_text:
ART. XIV.
Confutatur quinta sententia, quae est Timothei Bright Cantabrigiensis.

1. Cum extremam manum huic disputationi admovebam, cum acutissimi Timothei Brighti Cantabrigiensis librum de Sanitate, de Morbo, & de Morte, in manus meas incidit; in quo ille novam & insolitam sententiam de origine animae proponit. Verba ejus haec sunt: Quibus respondemus, nec totam, nec partem animi parentum traduci, neque accidens aliquod animi rudimentum esse. Quid ergo? Sane substantiam quandam ab anima natam, nec totam ipsam nec partem, tanquam animae immortale semen, prolis animae futurae principium: & sicut semen corporeum de parentum corporibus decisum nec corpus ipsum, nec corporis aliquod membrum emittit, ita anima per semen animae fecundum, non per animam aut animae partem aliquam, traducitur in prolem: & paulo post, Ergo tenemus, animam ut integram & absolutam parentibus referendam acceptam; sed seminale quid ab anima, aeque atque a corpore exclusum, & tandem verbi illius virtute (sc. foecunditatis benedictione) in animam rationalem & immortalem proditurum.

2. Hanc sententiam clarissimi & doctissimi Timothei sic confuto. Primo: Spiritus ille seu semen spirituale, quod a parentis anima excluditur & emittitur, vere & realiter praeexistebat in anima: realis enim emissio praesupponit reale inesse; at spiritus ille non potest realiter inesse animae parentis: Ergo neque realiter excludi & emitti ab ea. Probatur assumptio: spiritus ille non potest inesse animae patris ut pars in toto, fatente ipso Timotheo; neque ut accidens in subjecto, idque quia est substantia; substantiae autem repugnat inesse subjecto; neque ut res in loco ambiente, aut in vase continente — talis enim modus continentiae & circumscriptionis naturae spirituali animae repugnat.

3. Secundo: semen illud spirituale vel fit ex tota anima patris, vel ex parte animae patris, vel ex nihilo: non enim potest fieri ex materia corporea, tum quia est spiritualis substantia, tum quia ipse Brightus testatur illud non ex corpore sed ex anima natum esse: non fit ex tota anima patris, quia sic anima patris tota in semen converteretur; non ex parte, quia anima est indivisibilis; Ergo ex nihilo — quod creationem importat.

4. Tertio: conversio illius seminis spiritualis in animam vel est conversio accidentalis, qualis est conversio seu mutatio qua homo malus convertitur & mutatur in bonum, & color albus in nigrum; vel est conversio substantialis, qualis fuit conversio uxoris Loth in statuam salis, & conversio ligni in substantiam illius ignis cui approximatur. Non est conversio accidentalis, quia inde sequeretur semen illud spirituale non differre specie & essentialiter, sed gradu perfectionis accidentalis, ab anima — hoc est, esse animam rationalem accidentali aliqua ratione inchoatam & imperfectam: hoc autem contradicit verbis ipsius Timothei, dicentis semen illud non esse actu animam sed animae futurae principium. Si vero est conversio substantialis, tunc vel fit per abolitionem totius, vel per abolitionem unius partis essentiae altera remanente.

5. Quarto: DEUS valeat semen illud annihilare, & eo annihilato animam eodem instanti ex nihilo producere; non patri sed DEO soli tunc animae productio adscribenda est — quod ingens absurdum est, si vera sit ipsorum doctrina de traduce.

6. Quinto: conversio seminis in animam non potest fieri per abolitionem unius partis essentiae, altera remanente: primo, quia inde sequeretur spiritualem substantiam seminis illius esse corruptibilem & capacem transmutationis substantialis, non minus quam corpora Physica; illa enim aboleri & destrui possunt naturaliter quoad unam solam essentiae partem, formam videlicet: secundo, sequeretur substantiam illam spiritualem esse compositam ex materia & forma Physica, aut in partes essentiales — nam de his solis verum est quod earum una destructa altera remanere possit superstes quoad actualem existentiam.

7. Sexto: generationem hominis fieri sine interitu seminis non potest, si semen illud spirituale in animam convertitur; forma enim seminis, i.e. anima, maneret — at conversio substantialis interitum prioris formae requirit. Unde concludo Brighti sententiam non magis tutam esse quam praecedentes.
english: Article XIV. Bright's fifth opinion is confuted.

1. As I was finishing this disputation, Timothy Bright of Cambridge's On Health, Disease, and Death came to hand, with a new opinion on the soul's origin. He answers: neither the whole nor a part of the parents' mind is translated, nor is some accident a mind-rudiment. What then? A substance born from the soul — neither whole nor part — as an immortal seed of the soul, principle of the offspring's future soul. As corporeal seed cut from the parents' bodies is neither the body nor a member, so the soul is translated through a fertile soul-seed, not through the soul or a part of it. The integral soul is referred to the parents as received; but something seminal is shut out from soul as from body, and by the blessing of fertility goes forth into a rational immortal soul.

2. First confutation: that spiritual seed truly pre-existed in the parent's soul — real emission presupposes real inherence — yet it cannot really inhere there, so cannot be really emitted. Not as part in whole (Bright admits); not as accident in a subject (it is a substance); not as in a surrounding place or vessel (repugnant to the soul's spiritual nature).

3. Second: the spiritual seed comes from the whole father's soul, or a part, or nothing. Not from corporeal matter — it is spiritual, and Bright says it is born from soul not body. Not from the whole soul (the whole would convert into seed); not from a part (the soul is indivisible). So from nothing — which is creation.

4. Third: conversion of that seed into a soul is accidental or substantial. Not accidental: then it would differ from the soul only by degree of accidental perfection — an inchoate imperfect rational soul — contradicting Bright's claim that it is not actually a soul but a principle of a future soul. If substantial, it happens by abolishing the whole, or one part of the essence while the other remains.

5. Fourth: God could annihilate that seed and in the same instant produce a soul from nothing; then production belongs to God alone, not the father — a huge absurdity if their traducian doctrine is true.

6. Fifth: conversion cannot abolish one essential part while another remains. That would make the spiritual seed-substance corruptible and capable of substantial change like physical bodies; and would make it composed of physical matter and form or essential parts — for only of those is it true that when one is destroyed the other can remain in actual existence.

7. Sixth: if the spiritual seed converts into a soul, generation cannot occur without the seed's perishing; yet the seed's form (the soul) would remain, and substantial conversion requires the prior form's perishing. So Bright's opinion is no safer than the preceding.

ART. XV.
Confutatas jam esse omnes sententias de traduce; item neminem ex isto numero posse tutius aut facilius explicare peccati propagationem, quam nos qui animarum creationem defendimus.

1. Qui putant animam esse ex traduce, & a DEO non creari & infundi, illi necesse habent asserere animam aut educi ex potentia seminis per concursum passivum materiae, aut produci ab anima patris absque concursu materiae seminis: nam inter haec duo nullum datur medium. Prior sententia a me confutata est, art. 3. & 12. Posteriorum modum loquendi in quatuor alios dispesce ac subdividere possumus: Si enim anima patris sine concursu materiae seminis producit animam filii, vel producit eam ex tota sua substantia, vel ex parte suae substantiae, vel ex semine quodam spirituali, vel ex nihilo: primum modum confutavi art. 12.; secundum art. 13.; tertium art. 14.; et quartum art. 13. unde concludo, nullam dari sententiam de traduce quae non sit absurda & contradicens principiis sanae Philosophiae.

2. Jam vero ostendendum est, neminem ex Traduciariis posse tutius aut expeditius explicare peccati originalis propagationem quam nos qui animarum creationem defendimus. Meisneri ratio etiam sic concepta & limitata parum efficax est. Dicunt enim: Si anima a DEO creatur & infunditur, non potest peccatum originale in eam transfundi a parentibus, quia accidens non transit a subjecto in subjectum. At nos supra ostendimus, art. 6. & 7., quomodo singulae partes peccati originalis propagentur absque traductione animae: prima per naturalem generationem tanquam jus haereditarium; secunda negative, per carentiam justitiae quam parentes conferre nequeunt; tertia per dispositionem virtualem in semine, mediante sympathia corporis & animae. Quare creatio animae non tollit, sed optime conciliat, peccati propagationem.

3. Contra, Traduciarii, dum animam materialiter traduci volunt, in majora absurda incidunt: aut enim animam faciunt divisibilem & corruptibilem, aut parenti virtutem creandi attribuunt, aut semen spirituale inexplicabile fingunt. Quare tutius & facilius est, cum Ecclesia Catholica & sanioribus Philosophis, animam a DEO creari & infundi, & peccatum originale propagari modo a nobis explicato.

4. Finis Exercitationis Secundae. Sequitur Exercitatio Tertia, De Fide, Scientia, &c.
english: Article XV. All the adversaries' opinions on the translate have been confuted; none of them can explain sin's propagation more safely or easily than we who defend the creation of souls.

1. Those who hold the soul from a translate, not created and infused by God, must say either that it is educed from the seed's potency by matter's passive concurrence, or produced by the father's soul without the seed's matter — there is no middle. The first was confuted in Arts. III and XII. The second splits four ways: the father's soul produces the child's from its whole substance, or a part, or a spiritual seed, or nothing. I confuted the first in Art. XII, the second and the from-nothing case in Art. XIII, the spiritual seed in Art. XIV. So no traducian opinion stands that is not absurd and against sound philosophy.

2. No Traducian explains original sin's propagation more safely or easily than we who defend soul-creation. Meisner's argument, even limited, is weak. They say: if God creates and infuses the soul, original sin cannot pass into it, because an accident does not pass from subject to subject. But Arts. VI–VII showed how each part propagates without soul-traduction: the first by natural generation as hereditary right; the second negatively, by justice parents cannot confer; the third by a virtual disposition in the seed through body–soul sympathy. Soul-creation does not abolish sin's propagation — it best reconciles it.

3. Traducians who want the soul materially translated fall into worse absurdities: they make the soul divisible and corruptible, or give the parent creative power, or invent an inexplicable spiritual seed. Safer and easier, with the catholic church and the sounder philosophers: God creates and infuses the soul, and original sin propagates as we have explained.
4. End of the Second Exercise. The Third follows — On Faith, Knowledge, and related questions.
